```","language":"none"}],"urls":[{"text":"https://t.me/+GJ-FEpzcZrtmMTky"},{"text":"https://t.me/+GJ-FEpzcZrtmMTky"}]},"plain_text":"Claude Code has 7 instruction layers. Most teams use 1. In 2026, Anthropic made one thing clear: Claude Code is a systems problem, not a prompt problem.
Most teams still use CLAUDE.md for everything, but that creates context sludge, false confidence, and broken guardrails.
Here is the exact 7-layer runbook: CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, subagents, hooks, output styles, and system prompts.
Save this decision map if your Claude Code setup keeps getting noisier instead of smarter.
The mistake
CLAUDE.md feels like the obvious place to put every rule.
Claude reads it.
Claude follows it.
Problem solved.
Except that is not how long-running agent work behaves. Some instructions need to be present in every session. Some should only load when a file path matches. Some are procedures that should activate on demand. Some should happen in an isolated context. Some should not be instructions at all. They should be deterministic enforcement.
When all of those go into one file, you do not get a better agent.
You get a crowded context window.
The agent sees more words, but less signal.
The 7 layers
Anthropic’s official steering guide lists seven methods for instructing Claude Code behavior: CLAUDE.md files, rules, skills, subagents, hooks, output styles, and appending the system prompt.
The useful question is not “which one is powerful?”
They are all powerful.
The useful question is:
Where should this instruction live so Claude sees it at the right time, pays the right context cost, and treats it with the right authority?
Here is the simple decision table.
 
That table is the whole game.
The rest of this article is how to use it without creating a mess.
Layer 1: CLAUDE.md
Use CLAUDE.md for durable facts Claude should know almost every time it works in the repo.
Good examples:
 
Bad examples:
 
Those are not project facts.
They are procedures, enforcement rules, or guardrails.
The official guide points out the core problem: a shared CLAUDE.md can grow like an unowned config file where everyone appends instructions and nobody deletes them.
Every line loads whether it is relevant or not.
That is the hidden cost.
Rule of thumb
If Claude should know it in almost every task, keep it in CLAUDE.md.
If it only matters sometimes, move it down a layer.

Layer 2: rules
Rules are for constraints and conventions.
The important part is scoping.
Bad rule:
 
Better rule:
 
Now Claude only pays attention when the relevant files are in play.
Use rules for things like:
• migrations are append-only
• API handlers validate input
• React server components cannot import browser-only packages
• tests in this folder must use the local fixture builder
• docs pages need frontmatter
Rules are not for long workflows.
If the instruction says “first do this, then this, then this,” it probably belongs in a skill.

Layer 3: skills
Skills are for procedures.
A skill is what you use when you keep pasting the same checklist into chat.
Examples:
• code review
• release checklist
• debugging method
• security audit
• migration plan
• docs generation
• launch asset production

The key advantage is context cost.
The official docs say a skill’s name and description load first, but the full body loads only when the skill is invoked.
That means your 80-line deploy procedure does not need to sit in every session.
It loads when you deploy.
That is the difference between memory and instinct. CLAUDE.md tells Claude what is true about the repo. Skills tell Claude how to perform a repeatable job.
Good skill trigger
 
Bad skill trigger
 
The first one fires when useful.
The second one becomes noise.

Layer 4: subagents
Subagents are for isolated work.
Use them when the task would pollute the main conversation with too much intermediate context.
Good subagent tasks:
• search the repo for all auth entry points
• inspect dependency risk
• review logs
• compare three implementation approaches
• summarize a large PR
• audit a folder without editing it

The official steering guide explains that a subagent runs in its own fresh context window, and only the final message returns to the main session. [E1]
That is the value.
The main agent stays focused. The subagent can get messy.
A skill is a playbook inside the room. A subagent is another room.
Use the room when the work is large, noisy, or parallel.

Layer 5: hooks
Hooks are for deterministic behavior. This is the layer most people underuse.
If you write this in CLAUDE.md:
 
You are asking the model to remember.
A hook makes the harness do it.
Anthropic’s guide says hooks fire on lifecycle events and are useful for deterministic automation like running linters, posting to Slack, blocking commands, or backing up chat history on PreCompact. [E1]
That is a completely different kind of control.
A prompt is a request.
A hook is a mechanism.
Use hooks when “please remember” is not good enough.

The key distinction
Do not prompt what you can enforce. If a command must never run, block it.
If a formatter must run after edits, automate it. 
If a security check must pass, gate it.

Layer 6: output styles
Output styles are for changing how Claude behaves as an assistant.
Use them carefully.
The official guide notes that output styles are injected into the system prompt and can replace the default coding behavior unless configured to keep coding instructions.
That matters.
An output style is not a tiny preference.
It can change the whole role.

Good use cases:
• teaching mode
• proactive execution mode
• explanatory mode
• non-coding assistant mode
• strict review-only mode
Bad use cases:
• “use pnpm”
• “API handlers validate input”
• “run this deploy checklist”
• “do not touch these files”

Those belong in lower-risk layers.
Use output styles when you want to change the assistant’s posture, not when you want to store project facts.

Layer 7: appended system prompt
Appending the system prompt is for one-off invocation-level steering. It is useful when you want a temporary behavior without changing project files.
Examples:
 
Do not use it as a dumping ground for permanent rules.
If the instruction should survive future sessions, it belongs in a file.
If it should activate on a workflow, it belongs in a skill.
If it must be enforced, it belongs in a hook or permission.

The migration map
If your CLAUDE.md is already bloated, do not rewrite it all at once.
Move one class of instruction at a time.
Use this map:
 
This is how you shrink context without losing behavior.
You are not deleting instructions.
You are giving each instruction the right home.

The operator test
Before adding anything to Claude Code, ask five questions.
1. Should Claude know this every session?
If yes, CLAUDE.md might be right.
If no, keep going.
2. Does it only apply to certain files?
If yes, use a path-scoped rule or subdirectory CLAUDE.md.
3. Is it a repeatable sequence?
If yes, use a skill.
4. Would the work clutter the main context?
If yes, use a subagent.
5. Must it happen even if the model forgets?
If yes, use a hook or permission.

That last question is the most important one.
Anything safety-critical should not depend on the model remembering a sentence from earlier in the context window.

The common failure modes
Failure 1:  CLAUDE.md becomes a junk drawer
This is the default failure.
Every annoyance becomes another line.
Eventually the file is long, contradictory, and nobody owns it.
Fix: Give CLAUDE.md an owner.
Keep it short.
Review changes like code.
Move procedures into skills.
Move enforcement into hooks.

Failure 2:  Skills are too broad
A skill with a vague description fires too often.
“Use for coding” is useless.
“Use when reviewing code for vulnerabilities, auth gaps, exposed secrets, or deployment risk” is useful.
Fix: Describe the trigger condition, not the topic.

Failure 3: Hooks become invisible magic
Hooks are powerful because they bypass the model.
That is also why they can confuse people.
If a hook blocks a command, the developer needs to understand why.
Fix: Make hook errors explicit.
Document what each hook does.
Keep hook behavior boring.

Failure 4: subagents get used for everything
Subagents are great for isolated work.
They are not a replacement for clear instructions.
If you need to watch and steer the exact steps, use a skill in the main thread.
If you only need a result, use a subagent. 

Failure 5: output styles overwrite the coding assistant
This is subtle. A custom output style can remove default software-engineering behavior if you are not careful.
Fix: Use output styles for major posture changes only.
For project rules, use project rules.

The setup I would start with
If I were setting up Claude Code for a serious repo today, I would start with this:
1. A short root CLAUDE.md
Include:
• repo map
• package manager
• build commands
• test commands
• protected files
• what “done” means

Keep it under 200 lines.
2. Path-scoped rules
Add rules for:
• API handlers
• database migrations
• frontend component conventions
• test style
• docs frontmatter

3. Three skills
Start with:
• debugging skill
• code review skill
• release checklist skill

4. Two hooks
Start with:
• block dangerous shell commands
• run formatter or linter after relevant edits

5. One subagent
Start with:
• read-only repo researcher

Give it read/search tools only.
Use it when the main agent needs a map before editing.
That is enough.
Do not build a 40-piece agent stack before the five-piece version works.
The real lesson
Claude Code is not one instruction channel. It is an instruction hierarchy. CLAUDE.md gives persistent project context. Rules scope constraints. Skills package procedures. Subagents isolate side work. Hooks enforce behavior. Output styles change posture. Appended system prompts steer one invocation.
Once you see the hierarchy, the setup becomes obvious.
The question is not:
“Where can I put this instruction?”
The question is:
“What is the cheapest, safest, most reliable place this instruction can live?”
That is how you stop building context sludge and start building an operating system.
If you could instrument one Claude Code bottleneck this week, which one would you pick first?
